utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-98-32-T, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Welcome to the new year, thank you for being here. We are in a very much larger court; I'm not sure that I feel very comfortable in it after being locked away in the shoe box for so long. We are here for at least this week, and we may have to change next week. Now, doctor, you're still bound by the solemn declaration you made when you were giving evidence before, do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you finished, Mr. Domazet, with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I didn't finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There is his further statement which I think could become an exhibit, rather than him having to give that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. In the meantime, we have handed over another additional report, if I can call it, by Dr. Vucetic. So I should like to tender it into evidence. I don't have the number at hand. It's D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Your next number, I believe, is 39, unless you reserved that number for something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I think that would be fine, D39.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That further statement by the doctor will be Exhibit 39. Mr. Domazet, I'm grateful that this is being done this way, because it's very much easier to read it. But there was one further matter that I raised with you just before the adjournment which I said had to be dealt with. That was the shape of the heel bone. You may remember that Dr. de Grave had something to say about the different shapes of the heel bones. It may be that you can leave that for Mr. Groome to raise in cross-examination but if you want to deal with it, now is the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. During the last hearing, that is roughly as far as we got, so perhaps we could look into that now before going on to what the doctor said in his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, doctor, you have certainly seen the findings of Dr. de Grave regarding the heel bone and the other bones around the heel which he considered to be relevant for this case. So, do you remember that part of his report and could you comment on it, of Dr. de Grave

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I remember. One might say that there is a certain difference viewing the x-rays nine years before and nine years after. Those differences are possible both morphologically, that is, in terms of the shape of the bone and the structure of the bone. Those differences may be attributed in the first place to the number of years that have elapsed, to which is a period of more than nine years, and these are quite normal. They are normal over this period of time and they are of a degenerative nature and also affect the structure of the bone so that can be the explanation. Another fact confirming that the same bone is in question is the question of traction that Mr. Mitrovic [as interpreted] was subjected to during treatment, and the traces of that traction according to the finding of Dr. De Grave match to the findings on the scar, and they fit in with the facts that we have concerning the treatment of Mr. Mitrovic -- I'm sorry, Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Doctor, you have certainly seen the significance attributed to Dr. De Grave to this, because at least according to my own understanding of his report, it follows that on the basis of his findings in the heel bones, he says that those cannot be the x-rays of the same person taken in 1992 and 2001.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to agree over a few points. The differences can be confirmed but they are not so pronounced nor of such a degree as to make it certain that these are two different persons, and that is why I am giving this explanation, that a time period of nine years is a very long period of time when there are changes in the bone structure of each individual, be he injured or not, both in the structure and in the morphology or form and shape.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean, doctor, that in your opinion these heel bones that you have examined do not lead you to believe that these are different heels, or rather different persons that were x-rayed, in view of the explanation you have just given?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is very difficult to make any conclusions based on the heel alone. We have to observe the x-ray of the entire extremity, and it would be extremely unreliable to claim that those are not the same person simply because there are certain differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Apart from this, in Dr. De Grave's findings, when he talks about difficulties in establishing the fracture planes, which is another very important part of his report, you also told us last time that you disagree with the way in which he established those fracture lines and fracture planes. So could you please elaborate on that a little?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Don't you think, Mr. Domazet, that we have got a very elaborate explanation already? If he wants to add something new to it, by all means. But the whole purpose of putting the statement into evidence is to save the doctor having to tell us all about it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, but you yourself suggested last time that the doctor, in addition to what he has already done, should also try to make drawings which would explain this better, and the doctor has brought with him drawings which explain his findings and with the help of which he will be able to explain, in practical terms, what he has told us in his written report. So that is why I asked him this question, because I thought that with the help of these drawings, it would be much easier for all of us to understand better his findings in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Domazet, but why don't you just ask him to produce them. Ask him to elaborate means he will have to tell us everything that is in the statement already. So just ask him for the drawings and then if he wants to add something to what he's already said, he will be very welcome to do so. I want to make it very clear that we do not want him to tell us simply what's in the report. Because it's there and it's in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Vucetic, could you please show the Court the first of the drawings that you have made, and could you explain the one entitled "Correlation of bone fragments at fracture site of tibia dated 1992." If you could place it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have copies for the Trial Chamber, and could I ask the usher to give them to you for you to be able to follow more easily?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. And have you given these to Mr. Groome already or is this the first he's going to see of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received them too just before arriving at court. The doctor brought them with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, until we distribute copies to Their Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome we will leave it until you've had a chance to look at them before we worry about putting them in evidence but you have no objection to him being asked questions about them now, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Vucetic, you have before you your first drawing, so will you please explain what it is it shows?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be able to understand what we are talking about, it is very important to explain the fracture itself. It is a spiral fracture with a certain shifting as is shown on this diagram of the x-ray from 1992. It is important to note the upper point of the lower fragment, the upper point of the fracture, and the lower point of the lower fragment, and the lower point of the fracture and this is shown in both these projections, the AP and the profile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sorry, doctor, let's just -- so we can note them on our copies. The left is the front view and the second is the profile, is that -- the one on the right is the profile; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, yes. Precisely. Because of the shortening that occurs because of a fracture, there is an overlapping, and these points shift and these overlapping surfaces are shown here with diagonal lines. I have also prepared a model to show the tibia. This is the internal side of the tibia, this is the front edge of the tibia, this is the fracture, which is a spiral one, and it looks something like this. When a fracture occurs, there -- a shortening happens and the bones adopt this position, and that is what we see here in two projections. So this lower point of the upper fragment and the upper point of the lower fragment overlap and in the measurement and determining which is the lower point of the fracture is debatable, whether it is the point at the top of -- at the bottom of the upper fragment or the top point of the lower fragment. And we will talk about that further, the same applies to the lower fragment. On this diagram, we can see comparative demonstration of the measured values by experts who have been analysing this fracture. We have the x-rays from 1992 and the x-rays from 2001, and the findings by De Grave are marked with one star; Dr. Bollen, two stars; Dr. Raby, three stars, and Dr. Vucetic with a plus. It is important to note here that the findings of the three Prosecution experts very frequently differ significantly, though they do agree that their finding is the same. I have also shown this in the form of a table. That is now before you. It is also of particular importance for this case determining these points of significance on the x-rays from 1992 is relatively simple but it is on those x-rays that we have different measurement results by the Prosecution witnesses. Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Vucetic, I notice that when referring to the Prosecution experts, you focus in particularly on Dr. De Grave and Dr. Bollen. He is not actually an expert of the Prosecution; he assisted Dr. De Grave. So that his finding, Dr. Bollen's finding was used within the testimony of Dr. De Grave, but nevertheless, are there differences between them? Because Dr. De Grave asked Dr. Bollen to do the radiological part as Dr. De Grave is not a radiologist but you still find differences between the findings of Dr. De Grave and Dr. Bollen; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In preparing this report, I used the documents signed by Dr. De Grave and Dr. Bollen and the other experts, and I took these figures from those documents. And those facts and figures are to be found marked here as well as the source from which they were taken. It is true that Dr. Bollen's report is a component part of Dr. De Grave's report, but I used Dr. De Grave's report of the 24th of July 2001 and Dr. Bollen's report of the 15th of August 2001 separately, and these facts and figures are taken from those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Vucetic, in addition to these drawings, you have also attached two photographs which are not linked to Mitar Vasiljevic's x-rays, as far as I understand, but simply as an explanation for your findings. Could you explain to us with the help of those photographs the differences in the findings of the various experts?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my previous testimony I pointed out that these differences probably emanate from different methodologies applied, which are not only different but were -- was often erroneous and that is why we have different data. What I would now like to show you has to do with the healing of the bone. Before I do that, could I show this? The bone heals not only by the gap between the fragments being filled in but also at the point of the fracture a new bone is formed in an elongated form which covers the healthy part of the bone, and this can be seen very well on these photos 25 months after the fracture and 40 months after the fracture, how the bone changes. And it covers an increasingly wide zone and covers the fracture so it is difficult to determine the exact point of the fracture. This can also be seen on this example taken from literature, and these two comparative photographs show how the callous or the healing of the bone depends on the method of treatment. The way Mitar Vasiljevic was treated, in those cases, the place of the fracture is covered up by the newly formed bone, and that is the situation that we have on the x-rays from 2001, and that is why it is difficult to determine the extreme points, the ends, of the healed fracture, and that is why we have such divergent results. I should also like to draw attention to the determination of the fracture line as was done by Dr. De Grave. We have before us a schematic drawing made by Dr. De Grave. He shows here the fracture lines or fracture planes on the x-rays from 1992 and 2001. This is the fracture line from 1992 and the fracture line from 2001. What is of importance here? To determine the fracture line, he used the upper point and the lower point of the fracture when determining the fracture line for the year 2001. When determining the fracture line for 1992, he showed the upper point of the fracture and the lower point of the fracture in 1992 and the lower point of the fracture in 1992, and he drew the fracture line below the upper point, this is the upper point, and this is where the fracture line passes through, which should pass through the upper point. So this is quite different from the method of showing the fracture line on the x-ray for 2001. And this certainly requires an explanation. The explanation that I'm able to offer is that he used only a part of the fracture line, the central one, which has a certain inclination which is of a different angle, and on the basis of that inclination of the central part of the fracture line, he drew this fracture line, which does not correspond to what it should be. Those would be my comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Vucetic, you have used this pointer to show what you wish to show us but perhaps that's not precise enough. Could you please make a sketch for us which would depict what Dr. De Grave concluded and on the other hand, could you show what you view as a mistake in terms of the angle that he perceived? So could you try to depict the explanation that you have just given us.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It will be difficult, though, Mr. Domazet, because as the doctor has pointed out, Dr. De Grave has ignored, he says, the top part of the actual fracture. He's taken only the middle part of the fracture. The point that this doctor makes about the line being in the wrong place, even on Dr. De Grave's figures and demonstration, is pretty obvious. He hasn't taken the top of the fracture even as he saw it, but the real point that this doctor is making, as I understand it, is that Dr. De Grave ignored the very top of the fracture. It may be because he was unable to see it properly. But that's another matter, and I'm not sure -- and he will have to redraw really the whole thing to express what he sees to be the main point. He's already drawn it now, I see, which takes it through the actual top of the fracture as Dr. De Grave has shown it. That, if I may say so, is a very obvious point but it's the other one which I think this doctor thinks is the more important one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. But to the extent to which I understood Dr. Vucetic, Dr. De Grave explained that he found the upper part of the fracture, which is also contested in this case, and the drawing does not correspond to that. That was my understanding of the present explanation given by Dr. Vucetic because it emanates from the drawing itself. And I think that he managed to explain in some way where, according to De Grave, this angle should be shown. I don't know if I have understood the point of what Dr. Vucetic was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all right. I managed to draw a line here which would correspond to the postulates that were put forth by Dr. De Grave himself and after all that is what is drawn here, but he did draw a different line when determining the fracture of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Vucetic, I think you brought yet another diagram which you haven't shown us yet and that is remodulation, if I remember correctly, so I would kindly like to ask you, could you show this diagram to us, the one that has to do with remodelling and could you please explain it to us?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The notion of remodelling or the reorganisation of the primary bone is something that I've already referred to. However, what is significant in order to understand the x-rays from 2001 when the fracture heals there is a restructuring of bone tissue, and therefore all traces of the fracture are erased as well as of the growing back of the bone. That is something that is always present and that goes on for years to a greater or smaller extent. That is what makes it more difficult for us to have a proper orientation in ascertaining the fracture line on the fracture after it healed ten -- nine years later, in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor. If you have nothing to add to these diagrams at this point in time, I would kindly ask, since they are in a way an integral part of your report, that they be admitted into evidence as part of D39, as D39.1 as far as this first diagram is concerned, and then the second diagram would be 39.2, that is, the second diagram that explains the difference between 1992 and 2001, fracture healing would be 39.3 and 39.4, and this last one that you explained would be 39.5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. They will be as indicated by Mr. Domazet. There is actually a list of them which came with the copies of the documents, Mr. Domazet, so we may put the whole lot in. We can put that at the end, that would be number D29.6. And there was the model that the doctor has prepared. Do you want to tender that as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection to Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We will make that D40, I think, as a separate one. The chart that the doctor has handed us is actually already in the statement, which is Exhibit D29, but this is a very much clearer version of it. It need not be made a separate exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is contained in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. You proceed, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, in the case of the type of traction that was applied in the case of Mitar Vasiljevic, Dr. De Grave said here in court that this must have been done by a doctor with vast experience in view of the way in which this was done. Can you explain to us in the briefest possible terms what traction is and whether that is really the way things stand as Dr. De Grave had put it? Because this was actually performed by a doctor who was still an intern at the Uzice hospital.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Skeletal traction is simple surgery. A wire, a very strong wire, or a nail, is pulled through part of a bone that is very accessible. The method has been applied for over 100 years for treating bone fractures as temporary immobilisation or permanent immobilisation until there is total healing. This procedure is taught to very young physicians or physicians who are doing their specialist training. This is one of the surgical procedures that they learn among the first in terms of bone surgery, and with which they start their own practice in the surgery of bones and ligaments or their specialization in this area. Complications are possible in this kind of surgery but they are quite exceptional, and they can always be avoided if due attention is paid to the way in which the procedure is carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Vucetic, this procedure, that is, traction, is it applied only when both bones are fractured or is it feasible when only the bigger bone, the tibia, is broken?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be said, when speaking of treatment by skeletal traction which is only one of the ways in which such problems can be treated, that skeletal traction is more necessary when both bones are fractured. However, it is equally applied whenever we wish to improve the position of the fragments, and to correct the shortening involved in cases of fracture.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I would like to ask you something else now, Dr. Vucetic. You personally have been working in such hospitals where such problems are treated, and I would like to draw your attention to medical reports that are made. What does fractura cruris mean when a patient is released from hospital, et cetera? Does that mean that this necessarily implies the fracture of both bones of the lower leg area, or is it possible that it may refer to only one of the bones in the lower leg?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fractura cruris is a notion denoting the fracture of the lower leg bone. It mostly refers to the fracture of both bones but in some cases, although I must say it is sometimes used imprecisely, to denote the fracture of the tibia only. It is more correct to write fracture of the tibia and fibula, rather than to denote it as cruris. Sometimes it seems simpler to put it that way. And it often happens in practice in our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When speaking of this practice of writing medical histories and discharge reports from hospitals, can you tell us whether it is usual to enter other specific details in addition to the date, that is to say, the exact hour or minute, that is to say, more specific information than the date itself, especially when speaking of the period that is involved here and, of course, referring to the later period until the present day?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say to you that it is very exceptional to find information on the minute and hour of the injury sustained. In most cases, of course, it is compulsory to enter the date of injury and also whether the injury took place at the workplace or generally speaking the circumstances under which the patient was injured are described. Only in the largest emergency hospital in Belgrade, when patients are received, the date, hour and minute are registered when the patient reported to the emergency hospital. Otherwise, this information is not registered in other institutions, in terms of minutes and hours. I am familiar with this because I personally receive patients for treatment, as does the institution where I work, where treatment had started in other institutions, and then, due to the nature of their injuries, their treatment has to be continued in the institution where I work, and I never find any information regarding the minute or hour of injury, either in the pre-war times or in the time of war or even now after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Vucetic, one of the important facts involved here was the question of refracture, since Mitar Vasiljevic sustained a refracture within less than a year after the first fracture, you saw this in the opinion of Dr. De Grave, and especially what he thought about refracture in two year periods. So I would kindly ask you to present your point of view with regard to this particular matter.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Refracture always occurs at the point where the previous fracture had taken place, especially within a period of less than one year. This can be explained in the following way. The place where the first fracture had healed, until there is definite remodelling or regrowth, is a weak point. Also, another thing that shows this, that refracture occurs at the point where the previous fracture had taken place, is the possibility of the appearance of some other fragments which does happen sometimes, probably as more time goes by, there is more of that, that is to say, more time since the first fracture had healed. So when there is a case of refracture, it occurs in the place where the original fracture had occurred, if there is more than -- if more than one year had elapsed since the first fracture, then we can expect more fragments, those that were not there in the case of the first fracture.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What about the treatment of refracture? Is it as a rule more difficult or, as it was stated here, much more difficult, than treating an original fracture?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are different fractures. The treatment of the refracture of a fracture that was difficult to heal, that took more than a year to heal, is indeed difficult. However, the treatment of refracture in the case of the fracture that was sustained by Mitar Miric [as interpreted] and where the treatment had been regular is not difficult. Practically, there should be repetition or rather extension of the immobilisation period of three or more months until the refracture heals.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Doctor, this period that is often referred to of one year or two years, is that due to the fact that this is the period of healing, so it is therefore important in terms of assessing whether there can be a refracture or whether there can be traces of that that can be seen later?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One year after the fracture is the period during which the fracture heals, and this is when a fracture heals regularly, in a regular fashion. So fractures that occur in that period would certainly occur where the first fracture had taken place or along that line. However, refractures that take place later may possibly affect other parts of the bone that have nothing to do with the fracture line.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Vucetic, you have certainly seen from Dr. De Grave's report and his testimony that the x-ray does not contain elements which would lead him to believe that there was a refracture. Could you comment on that, please?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When a refracture heals, it is not possible to establish with reliability whether it is a healed refracture or a healed fracture because the appearance is the same once it is healed, so it is virtually impossible to distinguish between a healed fracture and a healed refracture, especially it is not possible to establish that on the basis of an x-ray taken many years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. De Grave states that two years later it is not possible to say whether the leg was broken once or several times at the same place. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, looking at a healed fracture, after more than two years' time, it is not possible to establish whether the leg was broken once or several times at that particular place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Vucetic, when it is stated that a fracture is normal or normally healed, this -- does this notion exist in professional orthopaedic surgery or is it just an explanation for normal healing as opposed to any other kind of healing?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The concept of a normal fracture, as such, does not exist. There is a fracture resulting from a commensurate force in relation to pathological fractures. So we are talking of a fracture here provoked by a trauma which makes it a fracture. Then there is a normal or regular course of healing, then there is an extended course of healing or failure of the fracture to heal. These are the concepts known to orthopaedics as a science. Also, the concept of an irregular fracture is something that can be used only loosely or colloquially. There is an expression "irregular fracture line" which helps us to explain whether the line is spiral, horizontal or diagonal. These are the terms used in orthopaedics.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Vucetic, when you were reviewing the reports and the testimony of Dr. De Grave, you certainly noted his comments on the x-rays of 1992, which you yourself have been able to review, and his comments regarding the stickers or parts of stickers or labels found at the bottom of that x-ray. In view of your own experience and your work in hospitals in Yugoslavia or Serbia, could you comment on that and say whether this x-ray from 1992 that you have had occasion to see is unusual in any sense with regard to the labels attached to the bottom of those x-rays?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question. This was something that I noted prompted by Dr. De Grave's comments, and I inquired with a number of radiologists and doctors and x-ray technicians to find an explanation. They showed me the boxes where they keep the x-rays and the method of marking those x-rays. All of them agreed in the explanation that these are plastic parts, there are slits, there are windows on those metal boxes closed with plastic sliding covers, and on which it is possible to write out the name and the shape of those plastic windows, or traces can be seen on the x-rays. This is an absolutely customary procedure on virtually all x-rays that we see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In that case, could it be possible for these labels to be stuck on later? Have you checked on that too?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I put this question in the same way that you have just now, whether -- as to whether it was possible at all, not in the context that we are talking in here now, and the explanation I was given was that it is impossible subsequently to intervene on x-rays taken, to interfere in the sense of marking, covering up or correcting the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And finally, Dr. Vucetic, let me ask you: You have also had occasion to comment on the report of the radiologist from the hospital in Gouda.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That report left a very good impression on me for several reasons. It is the product of an expert radiologist, and that report fully coincides with my own findings. I would just like to mention in this connection two points from that report. A healed tibia fracture coincides with the original tibia fracture from 1992, and a second finding that the fibula fracture can be the consequence of a trauma from 1993. So that report fully coincides with mine and I agree with everything it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, is that report in evidence? I'm not sure whether it went in or not. That's the one from the radiologist in the hospital at Gouda, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That is the report which I received and which I gave to Dr. Vucetic for his review, among the other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But is it an exhibit; that's all I'm trying to find out. It isn't according to my list and it should have been, I think, because it formed part of Dr. De Grave's general approach but I'm not sure it was actually tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was not tendered, that the Prosecution that obtained the report and disclosed it to me, has not tendered it into evidence officially yet and in my opinion too it should be admitted, since it has also been reviewed by Dr. Vucetic, and I think it is significant for Mr. Vasiljevic's defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are you able to help us, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I do not believe that it is in evidence. I provided the report as soon as I received it because it would clearly be Rule 68 material. Under 94 bis, if Mr. Domazet wants to introduce that report, I would have to agree not to cross-examine. I would want to cross-examine this doctor from Gouda. There were a number of, I believe, obvious flaws in that report and in the methodology used. If Mr. Domazet is going to seek to introduce that report, I would want to cross-examine that doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I understand that but would you object to the tender of it at this stage? Subject to your right to cross-examine the doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well, then. 41, D41. I think, Mr. Groome, as a matter of convenience, seeing that the Prosecution has been in touch with him, you better arrange for him to attend, it may be difficult from Mr. Domazet's point of view to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I provided all the contact details to Mr. Domazet when I gave him the report so I thought Mr. Domazet might want to call him as a witness and that's why I provided that several months ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Domazet, it will be an exhibit but subject to you producing the doctor for cross-examination. If you speak to the Victims and Witnesses Unit, I'm sure they will arrange it for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Whilst we are on that particular issue, that document that you filed I think last Friday in which you raised the issue about visas, you had not in fact drawn that to the attention of the victims and witnesses section. I read it last Friday, I made inquiry and they said they had not been -- that you had not been in touch with them about it. Merely filing documents, I'm afraid, do not -- does not ensure that people such as the victims and witnesses section see them; they are only sent to the Trial Chamber. So if you have those sorts of problems again, would you please speak directly to the section? You can send them a fax, I suppose, but you have to send them something directly. Merely filing a document for the Trial Chamber will not do so. I'm not trying to be smart when I say we are not a post box. It's simply a matter of ensuring, if you want them to see it, that you take some steps to ensure that they do see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Vucetic, finally, on the basis of everything that you have been able to see and review and the testimony you have given, in your opinion is there any reasonable doubt that in this case, these are x-rays of two different persons? I'm talking about the x-rays from 1992 and 2001.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am personally convinced that these two x-rays are x-rays of the same person. That is, that they show one and the same fracture. And all differences and doubts, differences of opinion, are conditioned by the fact that the x-ray from 2001 was taken nine years after the fracture, and all the changes that occurred in the meantime have been such that it is not simple to compare the x-ray from 1992 with the one from 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just one more question, doctor: In your opinion, would it have been easier if there had been more x-rays from 1992 or, if I can put it that way, if the x-rays had been of a better quality?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We lack x-rays from a later period. It is customary for patients to be monitored over a period of several months during treatment, and also upon the completion of treatment, which was not the case here, so this is understandable up to a point in view of the circumstances and the conditions under which Mitar Vasiljevic has been living over the past ten years, and the material and economic difficulties that the health service has had, as well as his own personal attitude towards his own health.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I was referring to the 1992 x-ray, I meant that we only have one x-ray taken from one perspective so my question was: Would it have been easier to establish this if we had more x-rays taken from different angles, because from your testimony and that of others, I have gathered that it is very important, the angle from which the x-ray is taken especially with regard to the smaller bone, or the fibula.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All that is important, but I have to say that on the basis of the x-rays that we have from 1992, there are no signs at all, in fact, that the fibula was broken, which again is not unusual. I have even, to corroborate this statement, I have brought an x-ray from my own experience, an x-ray taken a couple of weeks ago, in which I have a fibula fracture, at the end of the fibula, and from one angle, the fracture can be seen and from another, that fracture cannot be seen at all. I have those x-rays in my possession here, and if there is a way, I can show them to you. You can see here the fracture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm afraid we can't see anything from here, doctor. You could try it against a white sheet on the ELMO but I doubt whether we will get very much from it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me try. You can see here the date when the x-ray was taken, the 24th of December last year, so what I am saying is that it is not rare that on one -- in one perspective we can see the fracture and from another perspective it can't be seen. That's my point. I think this will be sufficient for me to show it to you. What I'm showing you now is an x-ray, this is the fibula and the fracture is here, but it is not visible on this x-ray at all. With the tip of my pen I will show you the fracture line. This is far more visible when one views it directly against the light, but I have said all this to show that it is quite frequent for a fracture to exist which can noted -- can be noted only if an x-ray is taken from one angle and sometimes not at all. In connection with Mitar Vasiljevic, the fibula fracture in my mind is linked to his information about an injury in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Dr. Vucetic. I thought this would be my last question. My question was whether there is any reason to doubt that these could be the same person or two different persons, so I don't think you have -- I think you have answered my question. Thank you. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Groome just before you start, you should all have got a message that we are going to sit an extra hour a day as between 4.30 and 5.30. We are very grateful to the Court reporters and the interpreters for cooperating but we are desperate to get this case finished by the end of next week. Yes, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, we are about to take a break. I'll ask you a few questions, but if possible could you leave the two x-rays available that you tried to show us that I could look through the light during the break? Thank you. If you leave them on the ELMO and with your permission I'll look at them during our break.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, now I want to go back to, or start with something that you said that I found interesting. You said that -- well, let me ask you, as an orthopaedic surgeon, are you saying that it is not important for you to know the time when somebody was injured?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very important for us to know when someone was injured. When I was speaking about this, we do not get the information about the hour and minute of the injury but certainly we have to know when the injury occurred, how many days or weeks, but of course days, prior to the patient reporting to the doctor, so days are important. The hours are of a secondary importance if we are talking about this kind of fracture. If we are talking about injuries of blood vessels or if an injury involves -- affects the blood vessels, then also the hour is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when you testified that in your experience in Yugoslavia except in one of the largest emergency hospitals in Belgrade, it's been your experience that the time that a patient comes to an emergency ward is not recorded typically, is that what you've told us earlier in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hours and minutes, the day certainly, yes, but in the case history, we do not have information about the hour. We do have information as to when the injury was sustained and when the patient was admitted to hospital, but we do not have the hour when he reported to the doctor. I know that this is recorded only in the emergency centre in Belgrade when there is a special column that is filled in regarding the hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, let me read back a sentence of your testimony and it's at the bottom of page 14 and on to 15: You testified, and I'm quoting, "Only in the largest emergency hospital in Belgrade, when patients are received, the date, the hour and minutes are registered. When the patient reported to the emergency hospital." Do you recall saying that just a few minutes ago? You need to just say "yes" or "no" for the mike.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So can I conclude from that statement that in other hospitals in Yugoslavia, it is quite typical that the time that a person is received into the emergency room is not recorded in the medical records?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me make myself even clearer. What I have insight into is the discharge paper and possibly the case history. As for the protocol, the book, which is kept in the emergency service of other institutions, is a document that I don't have insight into. What I am claiming is that in the case history, the document that accompanies the patient, there is no indication or only very rarely, but as a rule there is no indication of the hour and minute of the injury when the injury was sustained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think we better take the break now and we will resume again at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I apologise for the late start. It's my fault. I got involved in something which was urgent and which, as always, takes longer than promised. However, we are back. Yes, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, I would just like to ask you a few more questions about the time before I move on. What you said at the end of your testimony before the break is a little bit different than what you said earlier this morning. At the end of the break, you said that it's rare to find the time of the injury, and what you said earlier in the day was that it was rare to find the hour and the minutes of when a patient was registered as having reported to the emergency hospital. So I want to return to my original question. Is it your experience that it is rare on these case histories for the time a person has reported to the hospital to be recorded?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word "time" in the Serbian language, so to speak, refers to time in the sense of the day or the hour and the minute as well, so perhaps that is the source of this misunderstanding. So there is the day when the injury was sustained and then there is the day when the patient reported to the doctor. However, the hour and minute are very rare in medical documents such as case histories and discharge papers. That's what I'm referring to. And that is what I usually have in my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now -- thank you for that answer. Now, are you saying that even if there is a space to record the time, that in your experience, it's left blank?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Often.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, doctor, I just want to ask you a few questions about your report. I'm just reading a portion of your report and I'm going to ask you if you could explain what exactly you meant. In your report you say the x-ray made on the 14 June 1992 of the lower leg is labelled with L in the circle in the bottom left part. And then you refer to a call number, and you draw attention to the fact that Dr. De Grave did not see a call number also written on the x-ray. Do you recall what -- do you know what I'm speaking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call or code? I'm sorry, your reported as having said call.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, I'll read the precise quote from the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Groome, can you move your microphone a bit closer? We are getting a terrible echo here. Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The report says, "The black marker is poorly visible in the dark part of the x-rays so it is understandable that the expert witness, Dr. Yvan De Grave, did not notice call number..." and then you have a reference to Dr. De Grave. What call number did you notice that Dr. De Grave did not notice?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand this word that I keep hearing in the translation, "call number". I am speaking of the designation, of the designate. I'm talking about the front view and the profile or rather the left and right leg; "L" is the left leg, "R" is the right leg. That's what I've been talking about. That is what Dr. De Grave refers to as well in his report, and he also says that he could not find whether it was the left leg or the right leg. I found that designation and that's what I wrote about, and I imagine that this is what you've been referring to just now. Nothing else. Just this designation. That is to say, that it was designated that it was the left leg that was x-rayed. It is barely visible but it is visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, doctor, on your diagram -- and I'm referring to D39, I'm not sure what the suffix number is but it's the diagram of the entire leg, and what I want to ask you is on the diagram that you've provided us the fibula is on the left side of the bone, and yet on the x-rays the fibula appears on the right side of the bone. Can you explain why the fibula is drawn differently than the x-rays?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Excuse me, can I see the x-rays?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually may I see the x-rays.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, if I may, I handed up before the session the copies of the x-rays. I ask that they be distributed now to everybody. I will be using them in the course of my examination, as well as two other documents on. Perhaps it would save time to distribute them all at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: When you say, "Copies of the x-rays," you mean the two that you examined just before -- that you asked for just before the adjournment?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, not copies of those. Copies of Exhibits already in evidence. I believe it's 159 and 21. It's marked on the bottom of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that that all be given to the doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, I'd ask you to take a look at the photocopy of the x-ray that's marked P151 on the bottom. And on P151, we see the fibula on the right side of the tibia, yet on your diagram we see the reverse. Can you explain why?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the way it is. Basically, there is no difference. The x-ray that you have just offered, or rather the photocopy, according to the way it was oriented and according to what was written on it is the way these things are designated in medical documents, that is to say, in anatomy atlases and things like that, precisely the way you have just offered this. However, most often the left side is on the left side and the right side is on the right side. So there is no basic difference involved between the two. It depicts the same thing but it's just as if it were viewed in a mirror. It's not really different. It shows the same thing. It's just as if you were seeing a reflection in the mirror. What you showed me here is perhaps more correct in a medical sense but what I offered to the Court is perhaps simpler, for understanding what is on the left side and what is on the right side. This is the way things are in every day life, and it's easier for people who do not belong to the medical profession to view things this way. What is left is on the left side, what is right is on the right side. The fibula is on the left side here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me see if I understand you. What you're saying is that the fibula is on the outer part of the leg?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So this would be the view if we were looking down at our own legs, is that what you're saying? The view that you've done in your diagram on D39?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As in a mirror.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us what exactly just the word "cruris", what does that word by itself mean?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lower leg below the knee.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you also said at the end of Mr. Domazet's examination of you that in your mind you have no doubt that the x-ray from 1992 and the x-ray that we know to be of Mr. Vasiljevic from 2001, that they are the same person, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There can always be doubts. However, according to all the indicators that I managed to find and that could help me in this comparison, in this assessment whether it was the same fracture and the same x-ray, the conclusion was that it was the same fracture and the same leg and this fracture had healed since 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've told us in great detail all the indicators that -- you've testified about all of the indicators that the three other experts talked about, the indicators that they used to determine that it was a different person. Can you tell us specifically what are the indicators or the features of the two bones which you point to that are so similar that draw you to the conclusion that it is of the same person?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the form of the fracture. It is a spiral fracture, and that is not contested in the 1992 x-ray and in the 2001 x-ray. Furthermore, the orientation of the fracture, the fracture line also is not contested. Then also the localisation of the fracture. There are certain differences in the measurements involved that can be understood because we are comparing a fracture that was healed to the fracture as it was initially x-rayed. However, these differences can be taken as such. It can be understood as being one and the same fracture but after all this time, after the healing process, it is not exactly possible to recognise on the healed fracture what kind of a fracture it had been. Furthermore, the other parameters in terms of the form and structure of the bone do not involve such major differences that we could ascertain that these are different persons, or different bones rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But, doctor, you would agree with me that it's very different to conclude that it is impossible to say they are different people; that's a very different statement than saying that it is the same person. You would agree with me on that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, absolutely. These are quite different assertions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now let's talk about your assertion that it is the same person. Can you give us an idea about how certain you are of that? Are you certain that it's a 50 per cent probability it's the same person, a 90 per cent probability? Can you help us understand how sure you are that it's the same person?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is hard to put it that way. However, if necessary, in order to have a better understanding of this, I would place it at, say, around 90 per cent, 90 per cent probability.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, doctor, I want to move and speak with or -- ask you a few questions regarding the plane of the fracture, and I'd like to begin, you made some markings with a green pen on a diagram that you brought. I'd ask you to take out that diagram at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That was the copy of Dr. De Grave's schematic representation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, doctor, you made the mark with a green pen and unfortunately that will wipe off very easily. There is a black permanent marker in front of you, and I would ask you to retrace your mark with the black permanent marker so that it doesn't dissolve after you draw it. It was on the desk there during the break, the black marker to the far right, to the far right.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are the same quality.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With that marker I'd ask you to draw the general plane of the fracture as you would have determined it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Wait a moment, what he drew was what he says Dr. De Grave should have drawn on Dr. De Grave's own measurements. Because you'll see that the line Dr. De Grave has drawn does not pass through the intersection. This doctor has a completely different view as to where the fracture began and ended. So that if you are asking him -- this is of course what I think Mr. Domazet was also asking him -- he will have to now drawn into this Exhibit P21.3 where he says the fracture begins and ends before he could draft the plane or the general direction of the fracture, as he says it should be shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, the line that you have just drawn now, is that -- is the Judge correct, do you agree with what the Judge has said about what that line indicates?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Judge is quite right. He has completely understood this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you draw for us on that diagram the general plane that you believe that the fracture took? Can you do it on the diagram?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I'd like to say. This was marked according to the values measured by Dr. De Grave, and I am going to look at the values that I presented here for 1992, 5, 8, .4, and -- the differences may involve a millimetre. However, I think that it coincides with the line the way I draw it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's clear, could I ask you to put just "V" to indicate that you are in agreement with the line that you drew as being the approximate fracture plane of the 1992 fracture. Could you just put a "V" next to the line, in the same black pen? The black pen right at your right hand.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, could I ask to you draw an approximation of the plane of fracture that you observe on the 2001 x-ray of Mr. Vasiljevic? Can you draw that on the same document?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, the doctor is obviously writing on something which I think is plastic and that's why you are saying it's going to disappear. Would it be easier for you if he drew on the document underneath the plastic, which is a copy of Exhibit P21.3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Actually, what he has, Your Honour, is the image is on the plastic with just a cover sheet underneath it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Because I'm watching it on the screen here, it's like the Ganges river coming in and out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I was hoping to save a bit of time with starting with what he had already drawn but we can give him another copy of it if Your Honour thinks it's a better way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think you'll find it will be easier for him and for you if you just take a copy of P21.3, which is Dr. De Grave's schematic representation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only copy I have has a mark on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It was amongst the documents which you circulated this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, it wasn't, Your Honour, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm afraid my copy is very written on too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, perhaps the Judge is right. Let's move on to another area. We will try to get a paper copy for you to work with in the next few minutes, and we will come back to this. Now, doctor, in your report that you did in December, when you spoke about the plane of the fracture, you said that it actually changes somewhat as it travels from front to back of the bone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be put that way. If viewed in individual segments. The resulting plane is determined by the upper point of fracture and the lower point of fracture and a series of individual points are at a different angle. The fracture line looks like an extended letter "S", and therefore the angle is more or less slanted at different points. So the fracture line or the fracture plane is determined by the upper and lower points of the fracture. It moves from one point on the bone to the other, the opposite point, and that is how the fracture line is determined. If we were to follow the line itself the way it goes, and if we were to put a plane through that line, it could be in different positions. What I observed and what is presented here on the schematic of Dr. De Grave, he used one segment of this spiral which is clearly seen on the x-ray and which has this slant, this angle, that he shows. However, what is valid for us is this average value, the mean value, that is determined by the lower and upper points of the plane. That is to say, if we were -- if we could put a plane through this; that's what I've been trying to explain. I don't know how clear I've been.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think you've been very clear, and as far as the average plane or the general plane, we will return to that and I'll ask you to draw it. But for the next few minutes I want to ask you about the variations in the plane. And in your report, isn't it true that you say that at the front of the bone the fracture plane begins somewhat level and then sharply inclines towards the back of the bone as it travels to the back of the bone? Is that correct? Again, we need to hear your answer to be recorded.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That is the way it is approximately. It is hard, and perhaps it's not all that important for us to discuss individual segments of this line. What is important is that we try to simplify this line, which is of a relatively irregular shape but to put it in simplified terms, it has the shape of a letter "S". That is what is referred to in medical literature as well, this type of fracture. So in order to simplify this, and in order to make it more understandable also like this effort of Dr. De Grave's, was to present it through a schematic diagram. The point is that this plane is determined by the extreme points, the lower and upper points of the fracture, and that is what we should be referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay, doctor, let's talk about, go back to talk about the general plane. We now have a paper copy. I would ask that you -- you now have a paper copy of Prosecution Exhibit 21.3. I'd ask you first just to write your name at the bottom so that we'll know that it's your markings that you are making.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I'll ask you to draw two general lines and you can draw it and then we will place it on the ELMO for the rest of us to see. I would ask you to draw a line to indicate the general fracture plane that you observed in the 1992 x-ray.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would ask you to write the number "92" next to the line for 92, so that we know what it indicates.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, doctor, the two lines that you have drawn have similar fracture planes, and they fall somewhere between the two lines drawn by Dr. De Grave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. You have also here the values. That is, the distance in millimetres measured from the lower end of the tibia as De Grave measured, and here we have the values on the x-rays from 1992 and I have also drawn a plane for the x-ray from 2001, but the one from 2001 does not have the same kind of precision that we have determining the fracture plane for 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But, doctor, just for clarity, what is -- is there a name for the point in the tibia that everybody is taking these measurements from? Does it have a name? What is the name of the point in the tibia that both you and Dr. De Grave are taking your measurement from?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That point is the lower point of the lower fragment, the lower part of the tibia, the lower point of the fracture line of -- on the lower part of the tibia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm not talking about the fracture line but the portion, the reference point, that everybody is pointing to where the tibia, I believe, meets the talus?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I'm talking about. That point is on the fracture line so we are talking about the lower point on the fracture line, the lower point of the fracture line on the lower part of the tibia. And the upper point of the lower part of the tibia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, looking at the drawing that you have made or the drawings you've made on Dr. De Grave's diagram, it seems that the difference between the two diagrams is that Dr. De Grave has chosen a point higher on the bone as the beginning of the fracture or the upper most part of the fracture. Does that explain the difference between the two fracture planes?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a difference. Let me explain. I would agree with the findings of the Prosecution experts if, for the lower point, what they have marked as 8.4, if that is the lower point of the fracture on the lower fragment of the tibia. And with that regard, there is no difference virtually between my finding and the findings of the Prosecution witness. The difference does exist in the marking of the upper point of the fracture. There is a difference between me and Dr. De Grave. The difference is minimal on the x-rays from 1992, if you look.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, the difference between you and Dr. De Grave on the upper most part of the fracture is two millimetres; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is that accurately reflected on the diagram that you have just provided for us?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't. I have made a mistake. I shall have to correct myself. This would be 8.4. Yes. I have entered the correction now. So there won't be any difference but he'll see where the difference is. What Dr. De Grave offers as a line, he has drawn the line below the point through which I have drawn the line, so this is the line that he should have drawn. This is the line that he should have drawn. If he had drawn that line through the points that he has marked, then it would coincide with my own finding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main difference occurs in indicating the fracture plane on the x-ray of 2001, between Dr. De Grave and myself, regarding the fracture plane.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's just move slowly here. So you agree with Dr. De Grave's measurements of the 1992 x-ray. It's just that when he drew it on the schematic here, he made an error in the line? And you've corrected that for us?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could put it that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, doctor, let's stay with the 1992 x-ray for a minute. In your table that you provided us for the lower fracture point, you have two numbers, you have 5.7 and then you have 8.4 which is the same value that Dr. De Grave assigned to the lowest point. Can you explain why you have put two values in that particular box?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These two values show the following: The lower point of the fracture line of the distal fibula -- tibia, this is 8.4. That is, this point here that I'm pointing to now, the lower point of the distal tibia, that value is 8.4, according to my measurements. And according to Dr. De Grave. However, this point here, the lower point of the upper part of the tibia, is somewhat lower, and its value is 5.7.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you would say that the lowest point of the fracture is 5.7 and not 8.4?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when you drew the fracture plane the way you had described it for us is that you would draw from the lowest point to the highest point. Why did you draw it from 8.4 rather than 5.7?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a good question. And that is where there may be some dispute in explaining the fracture plane. It could be, or it should be determined by the upper point, and the lower point of the fracture line. However, as we have the situation that there is a shortening when a fracture occurs, there is a shortening, and if we are determining this fracture plane according to the upper point and the lower point of the fracture, it will be determined irrespective of the upper fragment, but if we put it this way and the lower point of the fragment will be lower down and that is the point 5.7, that is what we have here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor let me see if I understand you correctly. When the bone is broken we have two parts, the upper part and the lower part, correct? Let's ignore the upper part for a minute. The distance between the bottom of the tibia and the lowest part of the fracture on the lower part, that measurement is 8.4 centimetres, according to you, correct? Please yes or no.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that is the same measurement that Dr. De Grave calculated for that same distance, the bottom of the tibia to the lowest point in the fracture, correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, what you're saying to us now is, and perhaps if I could have the model that the doctor has made for us? Is that when a bone breaks, they overlap; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this other measurement that you have, 5.7, is the distance between the lowest point of the upper bone to the same reference on the tibia, correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, doctor, when Mr. Vasiljevic was put in traction, the whole idea of the traction was to drawback the bone so that it resumed its original place, correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the distance that hasn't changed is the distance between the bottom of the tibia to the bottom of the or the lowest point in the fracture of the bottom fragment of the bone, the 8.4, that has not changed, correct? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about the 1992 x-rays? Are we still talking about those.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just the 1992 x-ray, okay? So the measurement that will never change is the measurement from the bottom of the tibia to the lower most portion of the fracture on the lower fragment of the bone, correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. The lower fragment, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the measurement that you have, 5.7, that measurement could change depending on whether we were pulling back or forth on the bone, correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So would you agree with me that the better measurement for us to use in the analysis of this bone is the measurement that 8.4 that both you and Dr. De Grave put in your values? Correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about the x-rays from 1992, then there is no doubt that that is so, but the point on the x-ray from 2002 is something that we cannot see well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Let's just confine ourselves to 1992. So both you and Dr. De Grave have the same measurement for the lower -- lowest point of the fracture and your value for the uppermost part of the fracture, the difference is minimal, it's 2 millimetres, correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you would agree with Dr. De Grave's findings regarding the plane of the fracture in 1992?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, --

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But in as far as the designation of the points is concerned, but the plane he has drawn and the graphic presentation by Dr. De Grave does not correspond and does not coincide with the values he himself measured.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you've corrected that for us on the exhibit. Okay?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, and what you're telling us about the 2001 x-ray is that you are able to draw a similar plane or you are unable to because the bone has changed?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To do that with precision is extremely difficult. We can draw a line which can help us to make a comparison but to do so with precision is very difficult to do, and we can only determine a range within which that plane may be. An approximation, in other words, an approximate value can be given.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So I'd ask you on -- I'm sorry, I'd ask you to look at the angle of plane that you've written on your -- that exhibit in front of you and do you still say that that is the best estimate that you can give regarding the plane of the fracture in the 2001 x-ray?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have done here, the line drawn on this diagram, is an orientation, a visual presentation of the data that we have. It would require more precision if we were to compare these lines but on the basis of the values given in the table, which is a component part of the document, it is possible to make a graphic presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the difference between your findings and Dr. De Grave's findings, on the 2001 x-ray is -- are or is that you believe he's estimated the highest point on the fracture to be too high; is that correct? You believe he's picked a point higher than the actual fracture was?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when you look at the point of the bone that is 20.3 centimetres above the bottom of the tibia, you see no evidence of any fracture having been at that location; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way you put it, evidence that there was a fracture, by means of x-rays, there are signs of bone reaction. That bone reaction has manifested itself with the formation of new bone and that newly formed bone or callous appears where the injury occurred, that is where the fracture occurred, and covers a broader area than the actual fracture point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now let me ask you a question about that principle. What is the greatest distance that you would expect to see a change in the bone past a fracture, so if a fracture is, let's say, at 0, would we expect to see a change in the bone 1 centimetre above it, 1.5 centimetres? What is the distance we would expect to see a reaction in the bone above the fracture?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That distance may be half a centimetre, 1 centimetre or 2 centimetres as can be seen on this example that I'm showing you. You can see the fracture line, you can see the newly formed bone, and here it is indicated that this was taken 25 months after fracture and the other one 40 months after fracture, and you can see for yourself the difference and the changes that occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, doctor, what would be the typical -- you've given us a range. What would be the maximum amount of distance that you would expect to see bone reaction from a fracture? Is 2 centimetres the maximum distance?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could agree that it could be 2 centimetres or a little more on one side of the fracture line and as much on the other side of the fracture line so if Dr. De Grave fixed the point or a value of 20.3 centimetres as the highest point where he saw bone reaction we can safely say that the fracture must have been at least 18.3 centimetres above the bottom of the tibia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR VUCETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We cannot assert that but an assumption may be such as what I have said that that point is fixed at 16.5 centimetres. I may also have made an error, perhaps, because this is just an estimate made by whoever is doing the analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
