So this is one of the ways in which we can see that either his attention level dropped at that point or perhaps he simply did not understand some of the questions sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now that we are on the question of this test, what are the other ways in which this test can be helpful to you when establishing your diagnosis?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC
utterances.text: At this test, I got not only confirmation, which was to be expected, that he is a person who took alcohol. I also got another table that showed alcohol intake and this shows chronologically when the drinking started, the kind of alcoholic drink that he took and also what we call complications that may occur or rather what the consequences of the drinking were. I have attached this to my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In addition to these tests that you carried out, during those two days, you had conversations with him. Did he cooperate with you, and what is your assessment of his answers and also what he had to say in response to your questions?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic showed a readiness to talk. He was very cooperative. I think that when we first met I had a threefold interpretation of everything that happened. I'm going to tell you now how I interpreted his readiness. He met me and offered me coffee, fruit juice. He asked me whether I was hungry. He had something to eat. He wiped the table clean. He was preparing this. He was doing all of this in a bit of haste. So my interpretation of this was that he was tense, that he was anxious, that he is expecting something that is new to him, and this is a normal reaction to such situations. On the other hand, I did not forget that that is his vocation, that he is a waiter, and perhaps this is also a learned pattern of behaviour from that period. And thirdly, there was something that left the impression that he is a person who in a way does not hesitate, does not really have any breaks of this sort, in his stream of associations he would digress, go into details, which, for me at that point in time, were perhaps not even important but it was hard to interrupt him once he'd start talking, so he was a bit hasty. However, soon afterwards, when I was setting the guidelines, so to speak, when I said that we'd sit down and have a cup of coffee and we'd talk then, he immediately accepted that and then we started a conversation that was spontaneous. I was given -- I was giving the initiative, and I was also, as I said, setting the guidelines for this conversation altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Lopicic, when talking about the written documents, about the case histories that you looked at, do you recall, did you see, those documents from the psychiatry ward in 1992? I'm referring to therapy lists and everything else that he then had, both as therapy and, generally speaking, during the period of his treatment?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did see that, and that is the part which, for us psychiatrists and in clinical practice in general, was a diagnostic question. We often give sedation to delirious patients, and this has been said in heminephrine [phoen] and other such medication. We usually do not give neuroleptics primarily. In these discharge papers, I saw that he was receiving neuroleptic therapy. One should not also lose sight of the fact that 1992 was a year when we had major problems with drugs, with medicines. Unfortunately, this is an ongoing problem. So it is possible that the neuroleptic therapy that he received was therapy that was indicated due to the condition in which the patient was. It was required because he was very anxious from a psychomotoric points of view, and there is even documentation stating that he was affixed to a certain place and that is very rare in our hospitals. And may I just add that there is another thing that was included in the recommendations and that is that neuroleptic therapy was continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say "fixed," could you please explain this, what this means?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC
utterances.text: When patients are highly disturbed and when there is a major risk involved of them hurting themselves or someone else but usually it self-infliction. Then patients are tied usually across the abdomen. Usually there is a band that is put over the abdomen, but I imagine that that is the band that is usually used for this kind of affixation, as I said, and that means that his hands are free. And usually the patient is then in a ward or in a room where he is under the control of medical staff, a nurse in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned today that you inquired about Mitar Vasiljevic and that you got information from Dr. Simic as well, who at that time was a physician in the Uzice hospital; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you perhaps receive some information from him in respect of what he remembered, especially with regard to the diagnosis that was made then and what he and his colleagues testified about here, that is to say whether in that case, in the case of Mitar Vasiljevic, whether at that time he did or did not have delirium tremens?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC
utterances.text: The colleague I talked to said that this level of psychomotoric agitation was so strong that this can be seen in psychotic patients. However, I cannot speak on behalf of anyone else now, but my colleague was in a way inclined to interpret this by the energetic potential that was displayed, especially in terms of this psychomotoric restlessness. The assumption is that there was enormous fear involved, and this exceeded the usual level of delirious psychosis only. And also another factor that led him to believe that it was not only delirious psychosis was its duration. His estimate was that this lasted longer than deliria usually last.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I remember that I put a similar question to the other doctors who testified here and that they spoke rather exhaustively of delirium tremens and its characteristics, and they said that Mitar Vasiljevic did not have that at the time and they excluded that possibility. On the basis of the information that you have received can you state your view?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC
utterances.text: I have already said the clinical picture is untypical of delirium tremens, but it is also untypical for an endogenous psychosis. So it would be difficult to come to that diagnosis too. Now knowing the case history involved and having observed the patient over a certain period of time, we can say that it is certain that a significant role in the creation of this kind of psychotic reaction is displayed by the biological factor, but also, we should not disregard the factor of 30 years of alcoholism, as well as other circumstances that are no less important, that is the trauma he had, that is to say the fracture. In such situations a patient can go through delirium because of the pain involved itself. And here we have various factors including this biological factor, and of course there is also the factor of the living conditions involved and the stress under which Mr. Vasiljevic lived at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mrs. Lopicic, in your opinion -- you mentioned, first of all, that in your opinion, Mr. Vasiljevic is a psychiatrically changed person, with a psychopathology that was diagnosed, and you are of the opinion that this is proven by the documents already existing, and you believe that three factors were relevant in this psychopathology, you mentioned the biological factor, chronic alcoholism and stress. This changed personality of his, from a psychiatric point of view, and his illness, could it have been caused by one of these factors only or do these factors necessarily have to supplement each other, so to speak, or does one affect the other in such a way that it only aggravates the intensity of such an ailment?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC
utterances.text: I think that this situation was caused by a multitude of factors, absolutely. If we were to try to establish this through development, what he got through his genes when he was born and what he got through biology is the first, and then alcoholism certainly adds to this, which started at the age of 18, when Mr. Vasiljevic was 18. This is 1973. I think that this should not be forgotten. Yes, that's right, 1973. So all these years of drinking and also his living conditions later, the stress involved, and also the injury that was sustained towards the end of this period before the psychosis actually appeared as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean that this illness and this change could have taken place if we can imagine this, could have taken place even without the alcoholism, that is to say, even if he had not been an alcoholic, or is this just another factor that contributed to the aggravation of the illness and conversely, is it possible that this was only due to chronic alcoholism, that particular illness?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC
utterances.text: We could not say that it is only alcoholism if we are aware of all these elements, and now, whether this kind of a psychosis would have developed had it not been for the alcoholism, at this point in time, it is hard for me to say which form of psychosis and under which conditions. We are talking about a premorbid personality, a premorbid structure that we could discuss only after a psychologist had made his evaluation. We can speak of this hypothetically, that after a major stress, a psychotic reaction develops, the probability is there in this case because of the predisposition involved, but now, whether it would have developed as such or not is something I cannot say. I can only speak of what we have here and we have here 30 years of alcoholism, which gave a major contribution to the clinical picture being the way it is right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: With regard to this third factor that you have listed, the factor of stress, how does that affect the onset or the aggravation of the condition?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC
utterances.text: I mentioned this stress factor because when I was conducting the interview and when he was talking about the conditions of life at the time, he spoke about the fear, which was enormous, and which was heightening as the circumstances changed specifically when he was speaking about the period when he was mobilised and when he had to participate in obtaining food as part of the Territorial Defence and in organising the canteen, he was fearful because he had to pass through territories which were unsafe, and especially during a period of time when the front line changed and when he had to pass through the woods and other areas where the risk was even greater, and the very general circumstances of life, not just his own assignments but the living conditions were a stress factor. He had been separated from the family for a time, they haven't been transferred to Belgrade, he visited them. He took care of them but one must not forget that throughout that time he kept drinking more and more because he was alone and because he was more and more fearful, so it was a kind of vicious circle which he managed to close in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you were talking about these circumstances, you're talking about his personal circumstances, what he was doing, and the fear and stress he was under as a result. But were you also taking into consideration the general circumstances of an area swept by war, where there were killings and people disappearing and many other such events that accompany such an armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had that in mind because one of the reasons why he had moved his family -- they were separate for a while, his wife and children, were in the vicinity of Belgrade, precisely because he feared that something might happen to them because of those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And in your opinion, that also one of the factors contributing to this stress category. Would you include there in this category of stress the loss of a close relative or generally the death of other people to whom he was not related?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the harms scale of stress, I don't have it with me here, but I can send it, one of the most stress-provoking factor is the loss of a dear one. So if on the scale, the numerical scale is zero to 100 then this loss carries 100 points. Of course it depends on the closeness to that person. So certainly the loss of this person, who was a cousin, certainly affected his condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, but my question included other persons, should they be friends or colleagues or people that he was close to in the past. So would the loss of those people also contribute to such a deterioration?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC
utterances.text: It certainly has an influence, but depending on the emotional link, the greater the loss, and the closer we are to the person we are losing, the stress is greater. There is a direct correlation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When we are talking about such a loss or a death, in most cases a person is not present. He may learn about it and this may be stressful, But could being present at an event when, before his very eyes, in this case, Mitar Vasiljevic, people are being killed, whether he knows them or not, and especially if among them there are some that he considers close?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC
utterances.text: Certainly, yes, this is a stressful event. Any sudden situation which we cannot control and which provokes an emotional reaction from us is a stress factor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In your opinion, you have said that chronic alcohol abuse over a long period of time covered up the outbreak of possible affective or paranoid disorders and that alcoholism can be interpreted as a symptomatic and, in brackets, defence of earlier emergence of psychoses? Could you explain this part of your opinion, which is a medical one and we are laymen?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC
utterances.text: I had in mind, in the first place, the existence of this biological factor and the very fact about his mother, and I repeat, and wish to emphasise because I consider it to be very important, a mother who kills herself two months after childbirth. This can only be done by a person who is sick. We know very well what the relationship between a mother and child is, and what it means to leave somebody who is so totally helpless. So for me, this was a piece of information that I attach very great importance to, even now. If we were to assume, and we have been told, that she committed suicide, that she was treated, that she was sick, that she was psychotic, that she suffered from affective psychosis, then this was one much my assumptions, that if chronic alcohol abuse had covered up the possible outbreak of an affective disorder, what I obtained from the interview with the patient, and that is certain changes in the thinking process, this is some unclear psychopathology where he had exaggerated ideas about the significance of, shall we say, birds. If he sees a crow, it's a bad omen. If he sees a dove, it's a good sign. And this -- these various actions of his could be attributed to this paranoid disorder, like he said that he could communicate with his wife subconsciously. So this is what I attribute to provoking these reactions on his part.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Further on, in your opinion, you said that you considered what you called decades-long alcohol abuse had provoked organic changes, and you mention the brain, the peripheral nervous system, the gastrointestinal tract, as well as permanent changes of personality, and that this period with manifest development phases up to the addiction phase can be followed chronologically. Could you explain this part of your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC
utterances.text: This drinking went on since 1973. What we have in the case history and also in some of the findings is that Mr. Vasiljevic provides the information that he had black feces. He didn't at the time have an explanation. It was probably due to bleeding from the upper parts of the digestive tract, but he attributed it to drinking Vlaho [phoen] which is a strong alcoholic beverage in dark -- which has a dark colour. It was black and that was his explanation why his stool was black. And when he had these gastrointestinal problems, he must have taken large quantities of what he called shampoos, which reduce acidity in the intestines, and he obviously tried to treat this bleeding problem in that way. As for the peripheral nerves, he said that he had big problems walking and that he had pain in his legs. He even said that he walked around like a duck, which is very frequent. And when I was there, I did make an examination, and he has painful areas in the lower leg, and this is very typical of chronic damage to the peripheral nervous system. As for the laboratory tests, these also speak of liver damage, that is, the gastrointestinal tract. These are all elements indicating damage due to long years of alcohol abuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In your opinion, you said that this psychotic period is obvious in hospital conditions, and you also -- you referred to information obtained during your interview. When you are talking about hospital conditions and your opinion about it, is it based on the obvious proof about his treatment at the time or is it based on the way in which that disease developed?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC
utterances.text: I am basing my opinion primarily on the psychiatric report from the time and that was given by the psychiatrist who examined the patient. Also, Mr. Vasiljevic did give me some data about the psychopathology that he manifested in that period and prior to coming to hospital. In his case history, there is not that much information regarding the contents, the substance, of his psychosis, not nearly as much as I obtained from this interview. In the case history, we were simply able to establish his disturbance, his disorder, in terms of orientation, incoherent speech and probably thought. The thought process was accelerated too. Was this the cause of accelerated speech? These are things that can be found in the report. But the other aspects and problems in the thought process, I would call them exaggerated ideas, with magical connotations, and we have no information about that in the case history. The information is obtained through the interview, and it relates to the hospitalisation period, but also even before he was hospitalised, when he had this urge to blink, which was linked to thought disorder and symbolism.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: With respect to this last matter that you referred to, that is that you obtained this information from the interview with him, do you believe that the information he gave you was truthful, since he -- as you said, you were the first person to learn about these things?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC
utterances.text: I have to say that my subjective impression was that the interview and the talk we had over the two-day period was extremely authentic. Why he didn't speak about these things to anyone else, I can only assume. He gave me a detail which he described as a prohibition from God but he's not firmly fixed on this, so I wouldn't call it an insane idea but an exaggerated idea. Because he was not under the influence of alcohol for so long, and since he was in a protected environment, he is now in a situation where he can distance himself from all these things and he does so. And he said, "I thought what I experienced then was not normal." And then he checks this out with me by asking me whether I think so too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is that what you are referring to when you say that the patient is now distancing himself from these contents?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC
utterances.text: Yes. He now has an insight into his psychological pathology.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: From the case histories, and I'm thinking, in the first place, of the one from 1992, you were able to see the diagnosis at the time, and you spoke about this mental disease, psychosis, which has several subsections and subtypes, could you tell us a little about psychosis itself, what it is, of course if that is what we are talking about, if that is the mental disease we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC
utterances.text: In very clear terms, psychosis is a condition when the patient is out of reality. A psychotic condition implies a disturbed relationship with reality, and that is the period that I referred to as the period of hospitalisation. He did not have a good connection to reality. A psychosis may also lead to loss of memory, so he need not necessarily remember everything that he did while he was psychotic or when he had this psychotic episode. In Mr. Vasiljevic's case, that is precisely what happened. He cannot link all the events during his hospitalisation and give a clear picture or a precise description. He gives a fragmentary information from the period when he was at the psychiatric ward. He remembers only that he was tied. He doesn't remember much about what he said or what he did. He just remembers that he was tied up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that it was possible and that it was typical of psychosis, to have a loss of memory. On the other hand, remembering certain facts or saying that he remembered certain facts, can they be fully reliable, less reliable, or unreliable as compared to the memories of someone who is not suffering from such a disease?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC
utterances.text: Just as a patient does not remember, he also may remember. So it is something dynamic within us. At one point in time, we can remember something, and at another point, not remember something. It depends on the focus of our attention, the effective condition, because fear can change the ability to memorise. Therefore, this is something that cannot be simply put. If he's psychotic, he doesn't remember anything; and if he's not psychotic, he does remember. It is very difficult to draw a firm line, but if we know that a generator for the development of a psychotic process is a state of fear, then this state of fear may, in a certain way, affect memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When I asked you this, I also had in mind those memories which he may refer to or what he may have spoken of at the time, as testified by other people, to what extent could that be reliable and correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC
utterances.text: If it co-relates with what other people have said, if somebody said that somebody did such and such a thing and he also says that that person did such and such a thing, then that is proof that that was how it was indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is it possible for those persons to accept something that somebody else has said? In other words, are they as, a result of their disease, easily influenced?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC
utterances.text: The degree of suggestibility can exist among certain psychotic persons but in this case, if we are talking about the degree of suggestibility, we are able to also link it to alcohol, because alcohol is something that changes a personality. Now I come to something that is very difficult to tell: What is the premorbidity structure and what is the consequence of such protracted alcoholism? But it is the fact that there is a certain degree of suggestibility. Even in my own opinion it may be due to loss of concentration, but what is characteristic of delirium tremens, one of the tests we give our patients, is to give them a completely clean piece of paper and tell the patient read out what it says there. And if you start with a first sentence or a word, he will continue as if he was really reading, and so this is one of the traits which becomes part of the character of an alcoholic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In addition, these persons, can they seek to be more prominent, to draw attention to themselves, to pretend to organise, to lead, and generally speaking, is that a characteristic of this kind of behaviour or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that that would be directly linked to psychosis. These are certain character traits which are linked to emotional maturity or immaturity, and it is in that context that we may say that some persons, such as emotionally immature persons, are uncritical, suggestible, inclined to make fools of themselves, to be in the centre of attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As for memory, you said that the period of his hospitalisation, that is when he was treated, that that is a period that he remembers very little about. You said that he remembers being tied up but very little else. In view of his medical condition at the time, would it be possible for him to talk about things that never happened or could have happened and which may have hurt him in a sense, because he makes such public statements under those conditions?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC
utterances.text: Very frequently, a patient claims -- their psychotic contents are not real, are not correct, that is why they are outside reality. Therefore, in a psychosis patients very often say things which absolutely have nothing to do with reality. Now, it depends how they systemise things. If they consider that they are being persecuted or something like that, this is not -- this may not be happening or correct at all. It depends, the content may vary but it is quite possible for people to say things which are absolutely not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would this apply only to the period of hospitalisation in 1992, for which you have the necessary documentation, or could it also apply to the period prior to that?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC
utterances.text: Not a single psychosis can manifest itself as if you were to press a button. For the development of any psychosis, there is a prodromal period, as we call it, a period when the patient is suffering from psychopathology which may not be manifest. And this is something that in this case can be said to have existed in view of the fact that alcohol as a factor was present throughout this period prior to the outbreak of the psychosis, that is one reason, and a second reason is the factor of fear, as something which could also precipitate, generate or trigger psychopathology. That was present too. And therefore, it is possible to say that there were certain signs and elements of changed behaviour but far more changed subjective experiences which Mr. Vasiljevic did refer to to some extent in this interview I had with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We will adjourning now to 9.30 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one quick point. The Prosecution received its report from its psychiatric expert before the holiday and -- in B/C/S and that was given to Mr. Domazet and filed. We just received a draft translation of it in English a half hour ago and the final translation will be done tomorrow. If it's of any assistance to the Court, we will provide copies to the Court of the draft translation, if the Court wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That would be of great assistance. I have put that to one side, that document, until we get something in English. It would be of great help to have it whilst this witness is giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It will be delivered to your legal secretary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
